2.4.1.examLens: The highest-yield topic in Measure. Expect to compute Cp and Cpk by hand, convert to sigma level and defects, and decide what to do from the pattern of Cp, Cpk, and stability.

worked.question: A process has μ = 102, σ = 2 (within), USL = 108, LSL = 92, and the control chart is stable. (a) Cp? (b) Cpk? (c) Sigma level? (d) Expected PPM out of spec, ignoring any shift? (e) Long-term DPMO under the 1.5σ convention? (f) Diagnosis, and what happens if the mean is moved to 100?
worked.solution:
(a) Cp = 16 ÷ 12 = 1.33.
(b) Cpk = min(1.00, 1.67) = 1.00.
(c) Sigma level = 3 × 1.00 = 3.0σ.
(d) Z(USL) = 3.0 gives 0.00135; Z(LSL) = 5.0 gives about zero. Total ≈ 1,350 PPM.
(e) Long-term Z = 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5, so about 66,807 DPMO.
(f) Cp (1.33) is above Cpk (1.00), so it is a centering problem. Centering the mean at 100 makes Cpk equal Cp = 1.33, about 4σ.

2.4.2.examLens: Know what "stable" means, why tampering backfires, and the correct fix for stable-but-incapable versus capable-but-unstable.

worked.question: Four situations: (A) points all within control limits, but 8% of output is out of spec; (B) a few points beyond the limits, but all output so far is within spec; (C) an operator adjusts after every part and the chart now shows wide swings; (D) the chart is stable and the process makes 100% good parts. Describe each and give the action.
worked.solution: (A) Stable but incapable: redesign or reduce variation; do not chase points. (B) Unstable, appears capable: investigate special causes before trusting any capability number. (C) Tampering: stop adjusting; leave common-cause variation alone. (D) Stable and capable: monitor.

2.4.3.examLens: For pass/fail and count data, convert defects or yield to a Z value and a sigma level, and pick the right distribution.

worked.question: A line inspects 600 units and finds 18 defective units. (a) Yield? (b) DPMO (treating each unit as one opportunity)? (c) Long-term Z and sigma level? (d) Cpk using the reference-sheet attribute formula? (e) Is this a defects or defectives data set?
worked.solution:
(a) Yield = 582 ÷ 600 = 97%.
(b) Defective fraction = 18 ÷ 600 = 0.03, so 30,000 DPMO.
(c) Tail area 0.03 gives Z ≈ 1.88. Sigma level = 1.88 + 1.5 = 3.38σ.
(d) Cpk = (1.5 + 1.88) ÷ 3 = 1.13.
(e) Defectives (pass/fail units), so the binomial model and a p or np chart.

2.4.4.examLens: The BOK names this topic without detail. Expect "which monitoring tool fits this situation?" and "what does this capability output tell you?"

worked.question: A capability report shows Cp = 1.50, Cpk = 1.45, Pp = 1.10, Ppk = 1.05. What does it say, and what should you do?
worked.solution: Cp is close to Cpk, so the process is well centered. But Pp and Ppk are much lower than Cp and Cpk, so the overall variation is larger than the within-subgroup variation. That means there are shifts between subgroups: special causes or drift. The process is not stable, so the capability numbers cannot be trusted. Put an Xbar-R chart on it, find the special causes, and recompute capability afterward.

2.4.1.a.title: Spec limits versus control limits
2.4.1.a.html:
• Specification limits (USL, LSL) are the voice of the customer: what the output must be to be acceptable.
  • Control limits are the voice of the process: calculated from the process data, showing what it naturally does.

They are independent of each other. A process can sit inside its control limits and still fail the spec, or be inside the spec and out of control.

2.4.1.b.title: Cp
2.4.1.b.html:
Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ within). It compares the width of the spec to the width of the process spread. It shows what capability would be if the process were perfectly centered.
Example: USL = 108, LSL = 92, σ = 2. Cp = 16 ÷ 12 = 1.33.

2.4.1.c.title: Cpk
2.4.1.c.html:
Cpk = min[ (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ , (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ ]. It accounts for how well the process is centered by using the nearer limit.
Example: μ = 102, σ = 2, USL = 108, LSL = 92. Upper side: (108 − 102) ÷ 6 = 1.00. Lower side: (102 − 92) ÷ 6 = 1.67. Cpk = 1.00.

2.4.1.d.title: Cpk is never above Cp
2.4.1.d.html: Cpk ≤ Cp, always. They are equal only when the process is centered on the midpoint of the spec.

2.4.1.e.title: Pp and Ppk
2.4.1.e.html: Pp and Ppk use the overall (long-term) σ instead of the within-subgroup σ. The formulas are otherwise identical to Cp and Cpk.

2.4.1.f.title: The defining difference
2.4.1.f.html: Cp/Cpk use within-subgroup σ. Pp/Ppk use overall σ. "Short-term" and "long-term" are shorthand for that difference.

2.4.1.g.title: Benchmarks and sigma level
2.4.1.g.html:
Sigma level (short-term Z) = 3 × Cpk.

  • Cpk 1.00 ≈ 3σ
  • Cpk 1.33 ≈ 4σ
  • Cpk 1.67 ≈ 5σ
  • Cpk 2.00 ≈ 6σ

With the 1.5σ convention, the long-term yield sits 1.5σ lower: Cpk 1.33 corresponds to about 6,210 DPMO, and Cpk 2.00 to 3.4 DPMO.
Cue words matter. "Long-term" or "with the 1.5σ shift" means subtract 1.5 from the Z. No mention of a shift means read the Z table directly.

2.4.1.h.title: Z values and defects
2.4.1.h.html:
Z(USL) = (USL − μ) ÷ σ and Z(LSL) = (μ − LSL) ÷ σ. Read each tail from the Z table and add both tails for the total fraction out of spec.
Example: μ = 102, σ = 2. Z(USL) = 3.0, tail = 0.00135. Z(LSL) = 5.0, tail is essentially zero. Total ≈ 0.00135, or about 1,350 PPM.

2.4.1.i.title: Assumptions
2.4.1.i.html:
• Stability is required for capability to mean anything.
  • The usual Cp/Cpk and the PPM estimates assume normality. For non-normal data you need a transformation or a non-normal capability model.

2.4.1.j.title: What the gap tells you
2.4.1.j.html:
• Cp much larger than Cpk: a centering problem. Shift the mean.
  • Low Cp: a variation problem. Reduce the spread.

2.4.1.k.title: Cpm
2.4.1.k.html: Extension, glossary only. Cpm (Taguchi) penalizes distance from the target. Low exam yield.

2.4.1.l.title: "Cp 1.8, Cpk 0.9"
2.4.1.l.html: The process is off-center, not too variable. Center it, but only if the chart is stable. If the chart is unstable, stabilize first.

2.4.1.m.title: Compute Cpk from raw numbers
2.4.1.m.html: Take the mean, σ, and both limits, compute both sides, and use the smaller. Do the arithmetic for both sides even if one looks obvious.

2.4.1.n.title: One-sided specs
2.4.1.n.html:
• Cpu = (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ when only an upper limit exists.
  • Cpl = (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ when only a lower limit exists.
  • With both limits, Cpk is the smaller of the two.

2.4.1.o.title: The decision matrix
2.4.1.o.html:
ChartCapabilityWhat to do
StableCapableMonitor
StableNot capableReduce variation, recenter, or redesign the process
UnstableLooks capableFix special causes first; the indices cannot be trusted
UnstableNot capableStabilize first

2.4.1.p.title: Capability on an unstable process
2.4.1.p.html: Capability indices computed on an unstable process are not valid. The correct first step is to find and remove the special causes.

2.4.1.q.title: Reference-sheet formulas
2.4.1.q.html:
The exam reference sheet gives:

  • Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6s
  • Z(upper) = (USL − X̄) ÷ s and Z(lower) = (X̄ − LSL) ÷ s
  • Cpk = min(Z(upper) ÷ 3, Z(lower) ÷ 3)

It uses the sample standard deviation s throughout.

2.4.1.r.title: Cpk from attribute data
2.4.1.r.html:
The reference sheet gives Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) ÷ 3, with Z read from the Z table.
Example: yield 99.379% gives Z = 2.5, so Cpk = 4.0 ÷ 3 = 1.33. Yield 93.32% gives Z = 1.5, so Cpk = 1.00.

2.4.1.s.title: Confidence interval for Cpk
2.4.1.s.html:
Cpk ± Z(α/2) × √[ 1 ÷ (9n) + Cpk² ÷ (2n − 2) ]. The same square root is the standard error of Cpk.
Example: Cpk = 1.33, n = 50, 95% confidence. Square root = √(0.00222 + 1.7689 ÷ 98) = √0.02027 = 0.142. Margin = 1.96 × 0.142 = 0.28. Interval = 1.05 to 1.61. Because it includes values below 1.33, you cannot claim 4σ capability with confidence at this sample size.

2.4.2.a.title: Stable means predictable
2.4.2.a.html: A stable process has only common-cause variation: the natural, built-in noise. It is predictable, so you can say what it will do tomorrow.

2.4.2.b.title: Special causes
2.4.2.b.html: Special-cause (assignable) variation comes from a specific, unusual event: a tool breaks, a new supplier lot arrives, an operator skips a step. It makes the process unpredictable.

2.4.2.c.title: Tampering
2.4.2.c.html:
Reacting to every small deviation as if it were a special cause makes the process worse. Deming's funnel experiment shows this: adjusting after each result increases variation. Leave common-cause noise alone and change the system instead.
Example: an operator re-tunes the machine after every part that misses target by a hair. The result is more variation, not less.

2.4.2.d.title: Short-term versus long-term
2.4.2.d.html:
• Short-term (within-subgroup) variation: the noise inside a small group sampled close together.
  • Long-term (between-subgroup) variation: the noise plus drift and shifts over time.

A stable process has long-term variation close to short-term variation.

2.4.2.e.title: Stability comes first
2.4.2.e.html: Stability must be established before capability means anything. Capability describes what a stable process can deliver.

2.4.2.f.title: Stable but incapable versus capable but unstable
2.4.2.f.html:
• Stable but incapable: predictable, but the natural spread is too wide or off target. Fixing it takes a change to the process itself (reduce variation, recenter, redesign). Chasing individual points will not help.
  • Capable but unstable: it meets the spec for now, but special causes are present. Find and eliminate the special causes.

2.4.3.a.title: Defect counts
2.4.3.a.html: For counts of defects per unit, use DPU and DPMO (Poisson thinking).

2.4.3.b.title: Pass/fail data
2.4.3.b.html: For pass/fail results, use percent defective and yield (binomial thinking).

2.4.3.c.title: From yield or DPMO to sigma level
2.4.3.c.html:
1. Convert to a tail area (DPMO ÷ 1,000,000, or 1 − yield).
  2. Read the Z value from the Z table.
  3. Add 1.5 for the short-term sigma convention.

2.4.3.e.title: Check stability first
2.4.3.e.html: Before interpreting attribute capability, confirm the process is stable with a control chart and special-cause tests.

2.4.3.f.title: Defects versus defectives
2.4.3.f.html: Counting defects (several per unit possible) points to the Poisson distribution and a c or u chart. Counting defective units (pass/fail) points to the binomial distribution and a p or np chart.

2.4.3.g.title: Sigma level from DPMO with the Z table
2.4.3.g.html:
DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 = tail area. Read Z. Add 1.5.
Examples: 66,807 DPMO gives area 0.06681, Z = 1.5, so 3.0σ. 12,000 DPMO gives area 0.012, Z ≈ 2.26, so about 3.76σ.

2.4.4.a.title: Monitoring with control charts
2.4.4.a.html: Ongoing monitoring uses control charts matched to the data: Xbar-R (subgroups of continuous data), I-MR (individual readings), p (proportion defective), u (defects per unit). Details are in SG-5.2.

2.4.4.b.title: SPC first, capability second
2.4.4.b.html: Monitor the process over time with SPC. Re-evaluate capability after a stable period or after a process change. Calculating capability indices over and over on an unstable process misleads.

2.4.4.c.title: Sampling frequency and subgrouping
2.4.4.c.html: How often you sample and how you group the samples decide what the chart can detect. Subgroups should be formed so that variation inside a subgroup is common cause and variation between subgroups shows change over time.

2.4.4.d.title: Run charts
2.4.4.d.html: When data are scarce or you are starting out, a run chart shows trends and shifts without requiring control limits.

2.4.4.e.title: Pre-control
2.4.4.e.html: Extension, glossary only. Pre-control charts use green, yellow, and red zones set from the spec limits. Low exam yield.

2.4.4.f.title: Which monitoring tool fits?
2.4.4.f.html: Read the data: continuous individual readings point to I-MR, continuous in subgroups to Xbar-R, counts of defective units to p or np, counts of defects to c or u, and a time-ordered view with little data to a run chart.

2.4.4.g.title: Five different jobs
2.4.4.g.html:
Do not mix these up:

  • Monitoring stability: control chart.
  • Monitoring conformance of output: are units meeting the spec?
  • Periodic capability reassessment: recompute Cp/Cpk/Pp/Ppk after stability is confirmed.
  • Sampling frequency: how often to look.
  • Reaction and escalation: what to do when a signal appears.

2.4.4.h.title: Interpreting capability output
2.4.4.h.html:
A typical capability report shows a histogram with the spec limits, the indices Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk, and PPM within and overall.

  • Cpk close to Ppk: the process is stable; within and overall variation agree.
  • Ppk well below Cpk: shifts or drift between subgroups. Look for special causes.

options.html: Accept the process as highly capable

Increase the sample size and recalculate immediately

2.4.1-4.explanation: Capability indices are not valid on an unstable process. Stabilize first.

2.4.1-7.explanation: Cpk is never above Cp. They are equal only when the process is centered.

2.4.1-8.stem: Which statement about specification limits and control limits is correct?

options.html: Control limits are set by the customer
Specification limits come from the process data
They are independent: specs reflect customer needs, control limits reflect the process
A process within its control limits must meet the specification

2.4.1-8.explanation: A process can be in control and still fail the spec, or meet the spec and still be out of control.

2.4.2-1.stem: A control chart shows no signals, but 8% of output is outside the specification. What is the correct response?

options.html: Change the process itself (reduce variation, recenter, or redesign)
Adjust the process after each out-of-spec part

2.4.2-1.explanation: This is a stable but incapable process. Chasing individual points will not help.

2.4.2-2.stem: An operator adjusts the machine after every part that deviates slightly from target, and the variation grows larger. This is an example of:
2.4.2-2.explanation: Reacting to common-cause noise as if it were a special cause makes variation worse.

options.html: Natural variation inside a stable process
A new supplier lot with different properties
The usual small differences from part to part

2.4.2-3.explanation: Special causes are specific, assignable events. B and D describe common-cause variation.

2.4.3-1.stem: A process produces 12,000 defects per million opportunities. Using the Z table and the 1.5σ convention, its sigma level is closest to:
2.4.3-1.explanation: The tail area 0.012 corresponds to Z of about 2.26. Adding 1.5 gives about 3.76σ.

2.4.3-2.stem: A team counts the number of errors on each invoice, where one invoice can have several errors. Which distribution and chart family fit?
2.4.3-2.explanation: Counts of defects per unit follow the Poisson pattern and use c or u charts.

2.4.3-3.stem: Before interpreting attribute capability, the process should be checked for stability.
2.4.3-3.explanation: Capability for attribute data, like variable data, is meaningful only for a stable process.

2.4.4-1.stem: A capability report shows Cp = 1.60, Cpk = 1.55, Pp = 1.00, and Ppk = 0.95. What does it indicate?

options.html: The process is well centered and stable
Within-subgroup variation is small, but shifts between subgroups make overall variation larger, which points to special causes
The spec limits are too wide

2.4.4-1.explanation: Cp and Cpk (within) are much higher than Pp and Ppk (overall). That gap means variation between subgroups, so look for special causes.

2.4.4-2.stem: One measurement of temperature is taken each day. Which control chart is appropriate for monitoring it?
2.4.4-2.explanation: Single readings with a subgroup size of one call for an individuals and moving range chart.

2.4.4-3.stem: A team recalculates Cpk every week on a process that shows frequent control-chart signals. What is the main problem?

options.html: Capability indices are unreliable while the process is unstable, so SPC and special causes come first
Control charts are not needed once Cpk is known

2.4.4-3.explanation: Monitor with SPC first and reassess capability after a stable period or a process change.

2.4.1-1.text: A stable process has mean 51, within-subgroup standard deviation 2, USL = 68, and LSL = 32. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-1.answer: Cp = 36 ÷ (6 × 2) = 3.00. Cpu = 2.83, Cpl = 3.17, so Cpk = 2.83. Sigma level = 3 × 2.83 = 8.50σ. The process is slightly off-center.

2.4.1-2.text: A stable process has mean 50, within-subgroup standard deviation 1, USL = 55, and LSL = 45. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-2.answer: Cp = 10 ÷ (6 × 1) = 1.67. Cpu = 1.67, Cpl = 1.67, so Cpk = 1.67. Sigma level = 3 × 1.67 = 5.00σ. The process is centered, so Cpk equals Cp.

2.4.1-3.text: A stable process has mean 200, within-subgroup standard deviation 1, USL = 206, and LSL = 194. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-3.answer: Cp = 12 ÷ (6 × 1) = 2.00. Cpu = 2.00, Cpl = 2.00, so Cpk = 2.00. Sigma level = 3 × 2.00 = 6.00σ. The process is centered, so Cpk equals Cp.

2.4.1-4.text: A stable process has mean 200, within-subgroup standard deviation 2, USL = 215, and LSL = 185. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-4.answer: Cp = 30 ÷ (6 × 2) = 2.50. Cpu = 2.50, Cpl = 2.50, so Cpk = 2.50. Sigma level = 3 × 2.50 = 7.50σ. The process is centered, so Cpk equals Cp.

2.4.1-5.text: A stable process has mean 50.75, within-subgroup standard deviation 0.5, USL = 54.5, and LSL = 45.5. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-5.answer: Cp = 9 ÷ (6 × 0.5) = 3.00. Cpu = 2.50, Cpl = 3.50, so Cpk = 2.50. Sigma level = 3 × 2.50 = 7.50σ. The process is off-center; recenter the mean first.

2.4.1-6.text: A stable process has mean 100, within-subgroup standard deviation 2, USL = 112, and LSL = 88. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-6.answer: Cp = 24 ÷ (6 × 2) = 2.00. Cpu = 2.00, Cpl = 2.00, so Cpk = 2.00. Sigma level = 3 × 2.00 = 6.00σ. The process is centered, so Cpk equals Cp.

2.4.1-7.text: A stable process has mean 51.5, within-subgroup standard deviation 1.5, USL = 63.5, and LSL = 36.5. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-7.answer: Cp = 27 ÷ (6 × 1.5) = 3.00. Cpu = 2.67, Cpl = 3.33, so Cpk = 2.67. Sigma level = 3 × 2.67 = 8.00σ. The process is off-center; recenter the mean first.

2.4.1-8.text: A stable process has mean 201.5, within-subgroup standard deviation 1.5, USL = 206, and LSL = 194. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.

2.4.1-9.text: A stable process has mean 100.5, within-subgroup standard deviation 0.5, USL = 102.5, and LSL = 97.5. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
2.4.1-9.answer: Cp = 5 ÷ (6 × 0.5) = 1.67. Cpu = 1.33, Cpl = 2.00, so Cpk = 1.33. Sigma level = 3 × 1.33 = 4.00σ. The process is off-center; recenter the mean first.

2.4.1-10.text: A stable process has mean 50.25, within-subgroup standard deviation 0.5, USL = 53, and LSL = 47. Find Cp and Cpk, the sigma level (3 × Cpk), and diagnose it.
